Transforming cybersecurity with agentic AI to combat emerging 
cyber threats
Nir Kshetri
Bryan School of Business and Economics, The University of North Carolina at Greensboro, Bryan Building, Room: 368, P. O. Box 26165, Greensboro, 
NC, 27402-6165, USA
A B S T R A C T
This paper investigates the transformative potential of agentic AI in cybersecurity, specifically addressing how it can enhance practices in response 
to emerging threats. It aims to explore how agentic AI can transform cybersecurity practices, particularly in addressing new and evolving threats, 
while also examining the cybersecurity risks associated with its integration. The research explores the possibilities for agentic AI to automate critical 
tasks within Security Operations Centers (SOCs), such as decision-making, incident response, and threat detection. It also emphasizes the risks 
associated with AI integration, including the introduction of new vulnerabilities and challenges in managing automated systems, which call for a 
reassessment of existing cybersecurity frameworks to effectively address these risks.

Introduction In 2024, the global artificial intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity market was valued at $24.8 billion. It is expected to grow to $29.6 billion in 2025 and exceed $146.5 billion by 2034 ( Precedence Research, 2024 ). Agentic AI, representing the third wave of AI, is expected to account for a growing share of this market. Agentic AI strengthens Security Operations Centers (SOCs) by analyzing large datasets of threat intelligence and improving the detection of real threats versus false positives. Large language models (LLMs) trained for this purpose offer real-time, contextual insights, saving analysts time ( Columbus, 2025 ). Agentic AI systems can autonomously detect, respond to, and mitigate security and fraud threats in near real-time ( CIO, 2024 ). AI agents enable personalized protocols that adapt to specific threats and vulnerabilities ( CIO, 2024 ). A network of specialized models, each tasked with identifying different vulnerabilities, share insights, and collectively address threats ( Institute for Experiential AI., 2025 ). For example, cybersecurity company Darktrace ’ s agentic AI, Enterprise Immune System, detects and responds to threats by learning normal network behavior. Rather than relying on security teams, it autonomously mitigates risks by quarantining suspicious devices or blocking unusual data transfers in real time ( Hoque, 2025 ). This capability reduces response times to potential attacks as well as costs, strengthening overall security by providing faster, more efficient threat management ( Castellanos, 2021 ) and enhancing system resilience ( Weigand, 2025 ). This streamlines workflows, minimizes manual intervention ( CIO, 2024 ), enhances SOC efficiency, and enables faster decision-making ( Columbus, 2025 ). Research and consulting firm Gartner ’ s report, Predict 2025: There Will Never Be an Autonomous SOC , forecasts that AI will enhance SOC efficiency by 40 % by 2026, compared to 2024. This increase in efficiency will shift SOC roles toward AI development, maintenance, and security, marking a significant change in how cybersecurity teams operate ( Columbus, 2025 ). AI is this soon expected to shift from chatbots to agent-driven cybersecurity, enhancing threat detection, autonomous responses, scalability, and cyber hygiene ( Weigand, 2025 ). As AI systems security teams may delegate tasks like tracking supply-chain weak­ nesses, maintaining system inventories, and handling alerts, improving overall defense capabilities ( Klappholz, 2025 ). Analysts also predict the growing prevalence of virtual CISO (vCISO) roles as organizations face challenges in finding and retaining top cybersecurity talent. Many businesses may turn to vCISO services to access high-level expertise on a flexible basis, which could democratize access to experienced cybersecurity professionals. This trend enables smaller organizations to benefit from expert guidance without the cost of hiring a full-time CISO ( Right-Hand AI., 2025a , b ). A KPMG survey of UK tech leaders found that half of the boards highlighted cybersecurity issues as a significant worry when adopting generative AI tools (Woollacott, 2024). Adversaries are achieving breakout times of just 2 min and 7 s, highlighting the need for faster detection and response in cybersecurity ( Columbus, 2025 ). The various benefits of agentic AI mentioned earlier are expected to help mitigate cybersecurity concerns. On the other side of the coin, with any new technology, existing threats persist, new threats emerge, and traditional vulnerabilities become more consequential ( Baker, 2025 ). Like other emerging technologies (e.g., Kshetri, 2021 ), agentic AI can also bring increased security risks. Unlike traditional AI systems that function within controlled environments, AI agents interact with various systems and external data sources, expanding the potential attack surface. This can lead to unauthorized access, data leakage, and other vulner­ abilities. Weak integration or system flaws have previously allowed sensitive data to be exposed, while malicious actors or coding errors can manipulate AI agents, causing unintended disruptions or financial losses ( Ramesh, 2025 ). If an agentic AI system is hacked, the consequences can be severe. First, detecting and confirming the breach may take time, and even a minor change can lead to significant effects. Second, the system ’ s autonomy introduces new security vulnerabilities that must be addressed. Finally, the greatest risk lies in deploying a system without proper monitoring, logging, and controls — these cannot be added as afterthoughts ( Kaufman, 2024 ). This paper analyzes how agentic AI can transform cybersecurity practices while also introducing security risks, addressing two main research questions.

sections.heading: RQ2
sections.text: . What are the cybersecurity risks associated with agentic AI? The paper is structured as follows. First, we introduce the concept of AI agents and agentic AI, discussing their functionality, evolution, and key differences between traditional AI and agentic AI. Next, we explore how agentic AI enhances cybersecurity, highlighting its applications and benefits in securing digital systems. Following this, we examine the security and privacy risks associated with AI agents, proposing a Risk Management Framework to address these challenges. We then analyze the malicious potential of agentic AI in cybercrime, exploring how it could be exploited for harmful purposes. Afterward, we discuss the broader implications of agentic AI on the cybersecurity landscape and the necessary steps for regulation. Finally, we offer concluding remarks. 2. Understanding AI agents and agentic AI: functionality, evolution, and key differences In this section, we introduce AI agents and agentic AI, highlighting their ability to autonomously perceive, adapt, and act, which plays a crucial role in shaping both cybercrime tactics and cybersecurity defenses. An AI agent is an intelligent system ( Boston Consulting Group, 2025 ) or a smart digital assistant that uses artificial intelligence techniques — like machine learning, natural lan­ guage processing, or reinforcement learning — to learn from data, make decisions, and perform tasks on its own without constant human input ( Carter, 2025 ), in order to achieve specific goals ( Boston Consulting Group, 2025 ). AI agents can retain memory across tasks, integrate multiple AI models to execute complex actions, and determine when to access internal or external systems autono­ mously. This allows them to make decisions and perform actions with minimal human intervention, streamlining processes and improving efficiency ( Boston Consulting Group, 2025 ). A consumer goods company used an AI agent to optimize global marketing campaigns, reducing the workload from six analysts weekly to one employee with results in under an hour. The AI agent autonomously gathers marketing data, analyzes performance metrics, and drafts optimization recommendations. After refinement and approval by an operator, it updates media buying platforms with the proposed changes ( Boston Consulting Group, 2025 ). AI agents operate through several interconnected modules to ensure effective functionality. The Interfaces enable communication with users, systems, and databases. The Memory Module stores both short-term context and long-term knowledge from past in­ teractions. The Profile Module outlines the agent ’ s goals, roles, and behaviors. The Planning Module uses AI models to develop actionable plans. Finally, the Action Module integrates APIs to carry out these plans. Together, these components allow AI agents to interact, learn, and act within their environments ( Boston Consulting Group, 2025 ). AI agents originated in the 1990s as autonomous software designed to navigate simple internet environments on behalf of users. With limited search engines and basic web content, AI agents were seen as useful for tasks like browsing, as the technology was not yet capable of handling the complexities of the real world. The rise of LLMs has spurred renewed interest in AI agents. Companies like Salesforce and ServiceNow are using specialized agents to automate tasks, analyze data, and personalize interactions. These agents leverage LLMs to understand natural language and determine when to call tools like web searches, code execution, and data retrieval commands, enhancing operational efficiency ( Hodjat, 2025 ). While both AI agents and agentic AI function autonomously, their capabilities differ significantly. AI agents are task-specific, operating within predefined rules to handle routine activities such as scheduling meetings or responding to customer queries.
